claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys can have dual-phase lamellar colonies with abundant internal boundaries.
Microcracks initiate at internal lamellar-colony boundaries and lead to brittle tensile failure.
A minor microalloying addition can preferentially segregate to lamellar interfaces.
Segregation of the microalloying element can reinforce lamellar interfaces against microcrack initiation.
The segregated microalloying element can act as an obstacle to dislocation motion.
A low microalloying concentration can preserve the overall dual-phase lamellar-colony architecture.
Suitable processing conditions can produce controlled elemental segregation at colony boundaries.
Microalloying-induced changes in interfacial chemistry can transform brittle or incoherent colony boundaries into reinforced, locally strengthened interfaces.
Interfacial segregation impedes the initiation and propagation of microcracks.
Dislocation pinning by the segregated element enhances yield strength without sacrificing ductility.
The microalloyed alloy will have higher tensile strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The microalloyed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
Delayed microcrack initiation and enhanced stress transfer across boundaries cause the predicted improvement in tensile behavior.
The beneficial effect is limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys with compatible dual-phase lamellar morphologies and processing that permits effective segregation.
Interfacial segregation through microalloying is a recognized strategy in some alloy systems.
